docs.title: ADR-0001: GitHub as the Single Source of Truth
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Date: 2026-08-03

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Context
docs.text: W7's knowledge is produced in two places: GitHub, where documentation can be versioned, reviewed and shared, and Obsidian ("Rafael OS"), used for fast personal capture of ideas as they occur. Both are useful, and both were already in active use before this decision was written down. Without an explicit ruling, it is ambiguous which one a collaborator, a future team member, or the founder's future self should trust when the two disagree.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: GitHub is the single official source of truth for W7. Any document, decision, or claim that has not been committed to the appropriate GitHub repository is not official, regardless of how complete or long-standing it is elsewhere. Obsidian remains in continuous use for personal knowledge management, but never as a substitute for GitHub, per Information Boundaries.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Obsidian as the source of truth, with GitHub as a periodic export. Rejected: this makes the canonical version live in a single-user, non-diffable, non-reviewable tool, which does not scale past one person and does not benefit from Git's history or review model.
  • Treat both as equally authoritative, resolved case by case. Rejected: this reintroduces the exact ambiguity this ADR exists to remove, and only shifts the disagreement to "which one wins this time."
  • A dedicated wiki or documentation platform outside GitHub. Rejected: introduces a second system to maintain, review and secure, without a clear benefit over Markdown already versioned in Git, and works against the open-format, no-lock-in principle in Technology Stack.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Every initiative under W7 knows unambiguously where to look for and commit official knowledge. Obsidian remains useful for exploration without needing to be "clean" or presentable. The cost is discipline: ideas captured in Obsidian must be deliberately graduated into GitHub before anyone else can rely on them, and that graduation step will sometimes be skipped by mistake — this is an accepted, monitored cost rather than an unknown one.

docs.title: ADR-0002: Layered Repository Architecture
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Date: 2026-08-03

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Context
docs.text: project-w7 needs to hold the philosophy, identity, governance and framework shared by every current and future initiative, while also being where WarTips (and whatever comes after it) is registered. As more initiatives are added, an unstructured, flat collection of documents becomes ambiguous about what depends on what, and what is safe to change without affecting everything downstream of it — the exact failure mode described in Architecture Overview.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The repository is organized into ordered layers — Foundation, Identity, Governance, Framework, Initiatives, with Products and Experiences living in each initiative's own repository — where each layer may depend only on the layers above it, never below. Concretely: docs/foundations/, docs/identity/, docs/framework/ (which includes governance), docs/initiatives/, backed by docs/architecture/, docs/standards/, docs/adr/ and docs/roadmap/ as supporting layers used throughout.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Organize by initiative first, shared concerns second (e.g., wartips/, homelab/, each with its own copy of philosophy and standards). Rejected: guarantees duplication and drift the moment there is more than one initiative — the opposite of "one fact, one home" in Knowledge Architecture.
  • A single flat docs/ folder with no layering. Rejected: works while the repository is small, fails silently as it grows — nothing signals which documents are safe to edit casually and which ripple across every initiative.
  • Separate repositories per layer (a w7-foundation repo, a w7-framework repo, etc.). Rejected: adds cross-repository reference overhead disproportionate to the actual size of these documents; folders within one repository are sufficient at this scale and can be split later if that ever changes.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Any contributor can determine the blast radius of a change by which folder it's in, without reading every other document first. New initiatives have an unambiguous place to be registered (Initiative Framework) without touching the Foundation. The cost is that this structure must be maintained deliberately — a document placed in the wrong layer (e.g., initiative-specific content leaking into docs/foundations/) undermines the whole model, so placement is checked as part of the Documentation Standard review.

docs.title: ADR-0003: Initiative Governance Model
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Date: 2026-08-03

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Context
docs.text: W7 is designed to work whether it stays a personal brand, becomes a consulting practice, a SaaS company, an education company, or an open-source organization (Constitution, Article VII). WarTips exists today as the first initiative; more will follow. A governance model was needed for how much autonomy an initiative has, and who can change the shared layers it depends on, before a second initiative or a second contributor makes the lack of a model a real, contested problem instead of a theoretical one.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Initiatives have full autonomy over their own products, voice and technology choices, inheriting the Foundation, Identity and Framework layers by reference rather than by copy. They do not have unilateral authority to change those inherited layers — such changes go through the Decision Framework, regardless of which initiative proposes them. Authority is assigned per layer in Governance, explicitly naming the founder as the current holder of authority at every layer, rather than leaving it implicit.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Full initiative independence, no shared governance. Rejected: this is indistinguishable from initiatives not actually being part of one ecosystem, and reintroduces the duplication problem ADR-0002 exists to prevent.
  • Centralized approval required for every initiative-level decision, including product details. Rejected: this does not scale past a single founder and contradicts the Constitution's Article V, which grants initiatives freedom to develop their own products and visual language.
  • Leave governance unstated until a second contributor makes it necessary. Rejected: an unstated single point of authority cannot be handed off, delegated, or reasoned about by anyone joining later — the cost of writing it down now is small, and the cost of not having it when it's needed is not.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: A future initiative lead knows exactly what they can decide unilaterally versus what requires going through the Decision Framework. Bringing on a collaborator or a second initiative does not require inventing a governance model under time pressure — Governance already has a role for them. The cost is that today, with a single founder, some of this structure is not yet load-bearing; it is accepted as documentation for a state W7 is designed to grow into, not evidence that this complexity is needed today.

docs.title: ADR-0004: Activate the Foundation Documents
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Date: 2026-08-03

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Constitution, Manifesto, Vision and Legacy contained the principles W7 already used, but each remained marked Draft. The ecosystem roadmap described the Foundation layer as complete, creating a mismatch between the authority attributed to these documents and their declared lifecycle state. Before activation, each document was reviewed against the Documentation Standard and completed with explicit Purpose and Context sections. The Manifesto was also clarified so its statement that W7 is more than a brand does not contradict the endorsed brand architecture used operationally.

docs.title: Constitutional Assessment
docs.text:
• Why should this exist? W7 needs an explicitly active source of authority for the principles inherited by every lower layer.
  • Who benefits? Current and future initiative leads, contributors and readers gain a clear distinction between governing principles and unfinished proposals.
  • Will it remain valuable over time? Yes. Explicit lifecycle state and recorded approval preserve the meaning and provenance of the Foundation layer as the ecosystem evolves.
  • Does it strengthen the W7 ecosystem? Yes. It removes ambiguity from the layer on which governance, frameworks and initiatives depend.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Activate version 1.1.0 of the Constitution, Manifesto, Vision and Legacy as the governing Foundation documents of W7. Their added Purpose and Context sections clarify intent but do not change the principles established in version 1.0.0. The Manifesto's description of W7 was clarified from absolute organizational and brand exclusions to the intended principle that W7 is not defined by any single company, product or brand expression. Future changes to their conclusions continue to require founder approval and an ADR under the Governance model.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Keep the documents as Draft. Rejected because lower layers already rely on them and the roadmap already treats the Foundation as complete, leaving their authority ambiguous.
  • Activate only the Constitution. Rejected because the Constitution explicitly depends on the Manifesto, Vision and Legacy to explain its beliefs, direction and long-term measure of success.
  • Activate the documents without structural review. Rejected because active Foundation documents should meet the Documentation Standard they impose on the rest of the ecosystem.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Every W7 initiative now inherits from an explicitly active Foundation layer. Changes to these documents carry the governance bar defined for Foundation decisions. The activation does not freeze wording forever, but future changes must preserve version history, document their reasoning and receive the required approval.

docs.title: ADR-0005: Activate the Endorsed Brand Architecture
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Date: 2026-08-03

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Context
docs.text: W7 needs an active identity model before additional initiatives or visual assets are created. The Brand Architecture already described initiatives as independently named brands with a visible relationship to W7, but remained marked Draft and used the mixed term "endorsed sub-brands." Its role also needed to remain independent of WarTips so the Identity layer would govern initiatives rather than derive its authority from one downstream example.

docs.title: Constitutional Assessment
docs.text:
• Why should this exist? Initiatives need a consistent way to express their relationship to W7 without losing their own identity.
  • Who benefits? Initiative leads, designers, contributors and audiences gain a clear ownership and naming model.
  • Will it remain valuable over time? Yes. The relationship model is independent of a particular visual style, product or technology.
  • Does it strengthen the W7 ecosystem? Yes. Trust and recognition can compound across initiatives while each remains appropriate to its own audience.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Activate version 1.1.0 of the Brand Architecture and adopt endorsed brands as W7's identity model. Every initiative keeps its own name, voice and visual expression while maintaining a visible connection to W7. Detailed visual identity remains deferred until a concrete use case exists.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Use one monolithic W7 brand. Rejected because unrelated initiatives may serve different audiences and require distinct voices.
  • Use fully independent brands. Rejected because the relationship to W7 would be invisible and trust could not compound across the ecosystem.
  • Keep the architecture as Draft until visual assets exist. Rejected because the brand relationship must guide those assets when they are created; it does not depend on them.
  • Derive the model specifically from WarTips. Rejected because a shared Identity layer must remain valid for initiatives that do not resemble the first one.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: New initiatives must preserve a visible connection to W7 but have room to develop identities suited to their audiences. Future visual identity work has a stable relationship model to express. W7 accepts the ongoing responsibility to keep the endorsement clear and consistent across initiative touchpoints.

docs.title: ADR-0006: Activate Governance and the Operating Frameworks
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Date: 2026-08-03

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Context
docs.text: W7's Governance, Decision, Initiative and Product frameworks already described how authority, decisions, initiatives and products operate, but remained marked Draft. Activating them required aligning the ADR criteria with every shared governing layer, making the initiative template canonical instead of encouraging copies of WarTips, and removing a claim that treated WarTips as a product before any product had been formally registered.

docs.title: Constitutional Assessment
docs.text:
• Why should this exist? Active operating rules are necessary to apply the Foundation and Identity consistently.
  • Who benefits? The founder, future maintainers, initiative leads and product contributors gain explicit authority and repeatable creation processes.
  • Will it remain valuable over time? Yes. The rules define roles and decision boundaries independently of current team size or specific products.
  • Does it strengthen the W7 ecosystem? Yes. Shared processes prevent duplicated governance, inconsistent initiative creation and orphaned products.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Activate version 1.1.0 of Governance, Decision Framework, Initiative Framework and Product Framework as W7's operating model. Significant changes to Foundation, Identity, Governance or Framework require the Decision Framework. New initiatives use the canonical initiative template, and products are registered under exactly one owning initiative.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Keep the documents as Draft. Rejected because WarTips and the roadmap already rely on these rules operationally.
  • Activate without resolving inconsistencies. Rejected because active frameworks must agree with the current initiative registry and documentation standards.
  • Use WarTips as the initiative template. Rejected because examples evolve with their own context; a canonical neutral template prevents accidental copying of initiative-specific decisions.
  • Delay governance until more contributors join. Rejected because authority must be explicit before it can be delegated safely.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: W7 now has an active path from significant decision to initiative and product creation. Future contributors can identify who approves a change and when an ADR is required. The framework creates process overhead for shared decisions, accepted in exchange for traceability and consistent inheritance.

docs.title: ADR-0007: Activate the Ecosystem Architecture
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Date: 2026-08-03

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Architecture Overview, Topology, Knowledge Architecture and Technology Stack describe how W7 is layered, where knowledge belongs and which tools support the repository. They remained marked Draft even though ADR-0001 and ADR-0002 had already accepted their central decisions. Activation required removing a fixed ADR enumeration from the topology and distinguishing open formats from replaceable proprietary hosting services in the technology rationale.

docs.title: Constitutional Assessment
docs.text:
• Why should this exist? W7 needs an explicit structural model so changes have predictable scope and knowledge has a canonical home.
  • Who benefits? Contributors and initiative maintainers can place documents, decisions and product work without creating hidden dependencies.
  • Will it remain valuable over time? Yes. The layer and knowledge models are independent of individual products, while the technology stack is designed for replacement.
  • Does it strengthen the W7 ecosystem? Yes. Shared architecture prevents duplication and preserves recoverability as initiatives multiply.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Activate version 1.1.0 of the Architecture Overview, Ecosystem Topology, Knowledge Architecture and Technology Stack. W7 retains its ordered layer model, one-fact-one-home rule, GitHub/Obsidian boundary and plain-text static documentation stack.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Keep architecture implicit in the folder structure. Rejected because folders alone do not explain allowed dependencies or change impact.
  • Activate only the prose overview. Rejected because the diagrams, knowledge rules and implementation stack describe separate aspects required to operate the same architecture.
  • Treat every tool as open infrastructure. Rejected because GitHub is a proprietary venue; portability comes from Git and open source formats, not from pretending the venue is open.
  • Keep the documents as Draft. Rejected because accepted ADRs and active frameworks already depend on these architectural rules.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Repository placement and dependency direction become active constraints. Official knowledge remains in GitHub repositories and private working knowledge remains in Rafael OS until promoted. Hosted services may change, but canonical content must stay portable in plain-text formats.

docs.title: ADR-0008: Activate the Shared Standards
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Date: 2026-08-03

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Context
docs.text: W7's Documentation, Engineering, GitHub, AI Usage and Information Boundaries standards were already referenced by active frameworks but remained marked Draft. Review found rules that were either internally contradictory or broader than the repository could safely apply: ADRs use a purpose-built record format, not living-document version metadata; not every initiative produces code; and Internal information should not be supplied indiscriminately to AI tools.

docs.title: Constitutional Assessment
docs.text:
• Why should this exist? Shared standards turn W7's principles into repeatable quality, security and review expectations.
  • Who benefits? Contributors, maintainers, initiative leads and readers receive consistent artifacts and clearer information-handling boundaries.
  • Will it remain valuable over time? Yes. The standards specify durable practices while avoiding mandatory languages, vendors or product architectures.
  • Does it strengthen the W7 ecosystem? Yes. Common quality and safety rules allow initiatives to remain autonomous without drifting below the ecosystem baseline.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Activate version 1.1.0 of the Documentation, Engineering, GitHub, AI Usage and Information Boundaries standards. ADRs retain their purpose-built template as an explicit documentation exception. Internal information may be used only with tools approved for its repository and handling context, while Private information remains outside Git and AI contexts.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Keep standards advisory or Draft. Rejected because active initiatives and frameworks already claim to inherit them.
  • Apply the living-document schema to ADRs. Rejected because decision records preserve a dated conclusion and have a distinct lifecycle defined by the ADR template.
  • Require engineering practices from every initiative regardless of output. Rejected because non-technical initiatives may have no code; the standard applies when technical work exists.
  • Allow Internal information in any AI tool. Rejected because classification without tool and data-handling controls would not create a meaningful boundary.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Shared W7 work now has an active minimum bar for documentation, engineering, GitHub collaboration, AI-assisted work and information classification. Initiative-specific standards may add constraints but may not weaken these baselines. Contributors must exercise judgment about tool approval and remain accountable for AI-assisted output.

docs.title: ADR-0009: Complete W7 Foundation v1.0
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Date: 2026-08-09

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Context
docs.text: W7's governing documents, architecture, frameworks, standards, and first initiative were active, but the repository still described itself as version 0.1.0 and left several identity and operating concepts implicit. Mission, values, principles of building, operating model, core color and typography roles, voice and tone, visual language, and the initiative registry required canonical homes before the repository could accurately claim a complete Foundation v1.0.

docs.title: Constitutional Assessment
docs.text:
• Why should this exist? A version milestone must correspond to an explicit, coherent, navigable body of governing documentation.
  • Who benefits? The founder, future contributors, initiative leads, and readers gain one complete baseline rather than reconstructing intent from scattered references.
  • Will it remain valuable over time? Yes. The documents define durable roles and principles while allowing assets, initiatives, and products to evolve separately.
  • Does it strengthen the W7 ecosystem? Yes. It closes structural gaps without inventing products or promoting candidate initiatives prematurely.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Adopt the expanded Foundation and Identity documentation, the canonical initiative registry, and aligned repository navigation as W7 Foundation v1.0. Foundation v1.0 means the operating model is complete enough to govern new work; it does not mean every future initiative, product, brand asset, or organization capability already exists.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Keep the repository at v0.1 until a product ships. Rejected because repository maturity and product maturity are separate concerns.
  • Treat the existing documents as sufficient and leave concepts implicit. Rejected because implicit identity and operating rules cannot be reviewed or inherited reliably.
  • Register all discussed future initiatives now. Rejected because names and ideas have not completed the Initiative Framework.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: The repository can identify itself as Foundation v1.0 and serve as the canonical baseline for future initiatives. New governing changes continue to require the existing Decision Framework. Production identity assets remain future governed work, and candidate initiatives remain unregistered until separately approved.

docs.title: ADR-0010: Adopt W7 Production Identity Assets
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Date: 2026-08-09

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Context
docs.text: W7 Foundation v1.0 defined the visual direction, palette, typography, and endorsed-brand model but deliberately stopped short of production logo files. The public documentation now needs a recognizable application mark, favicon, horizontal lockups, and social presentation asset that work across light and dark surfaces.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Adopt the SVG asset set in docs/assets/brand/ and the usage rules in the Logo System as W7's canonical production identity. The circular monogram combines a white W and gold 7 within a matte-black field, expressing balance without reproducing a yin-yang symbol. Black, white, and W7 Gold remain the only colors in the core mark.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Text-only W7 wordmark. Rejected because it does not provide a distinctive compact application or favicon mark.
  • Literal yin-yang construction. Rejected because the visual direction calls for conceptual influence, not reproduction.
  • Raster-first assets. Rejected because SVG remains resolution-independent, accessible, inspectable, and versionable.
  • Separate marks for light and dark backgrounds. Rejected for the symbol; only the horizontal wordmark color changes, preserving one recognizable core mark.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: W7 gains a consistent production identity for documentation and future initiative endorsements. Changes to the symbol geometry, core colors, or relationship between symbol and wordmark require an Identity-layer decision and a superseding ADR. Initiative identities may remain distinct under the Brand Architecture.

docs.title: ADR-0011: Adopt the Integrated W7 Mark
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Date: 2026-08-10

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The first production mark established the required asset formats and color system, but its closed circle and overlapping W and 7 remained visually separate. A subsequent concept exploration showed a stronger direction: one open circular journey surrounding an angular monogram whose letters share a geometric center.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Adopt the integrated open-circle W7 geometry as the canonical mark. The gold arc represents continuity and forward movement, the shorter white arc balances it, and the W and 7 converge without becoming illegible at compact sizes. The approved palette and asset filenames remain unchanged.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Keep the first closed-circle mark. Rejected because the parts read as assembled rather than as one identity.
  • Adopt the raster concept directly. Rejected because visual effects and approximate geometry are unsuitable as a canonical production source.
  • Use a fully abstract symbol. Rejected because recognition of W and 7 remains important at this stage of the brand.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Existing consumers receive the refined geometry automatically through stable asset paths. The open circle becomes a protected feature of the mark. Further geometry changes require a superseding Identity ADR.

docs.title: ADR Template
docs.text:
Version: 1.0.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This is the template every Architecture Decision Record (ADR) in W7 follows. Copy this file, rename it NNNN-short-decision-title.md using the next sequential number, and fill in every section before merging.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADRs exist to answer one question for a future reader: why was this decided, given what was known at the time? A good ADR is honest about the alternatives that were rejected and why, not just the conclusion reached. It is written when the decision is made, never backfilled to justify a decision after the fact.

docs.title: What Qualifies for an ADR
docs.text: Per the Decision Framework: anything that changes a Foundation, Identity, Governance or Framework layer document, creates or retires an initiative, introduces a convention other initiatives will inherit, or is otherwise expensive to reverse.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
# ADR-NNNN: <Short, specific title>

Status: Proposed | Accepted | Superseded by ADR-XXXX | Deprecated

Date: YYYY-MM-DD

Owner: <name>

---

## Context

What situation made this decision necessary? What constraints applied?

## Decision

What was decided, stated as a plain sentence, not a question.

## Alternatives Considered

- Alternative A — why it was not chosen
- Alternative B — why it was not chosen
- Doing nothing — why that was not sufficient

## Consequences

What becomes easier because of this decision? What becomes harder or
is given up? What does this commit future initiatives to?

## Related

Links to the documents or ADRs this decision affects or depends on.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: An ADR is never edited to change its conclusion after it is Accepted. If circumstances change, a new ADR is written, marked Superseded by ADR-XXXX, and the old one is updated only to add that status line — its original reasoning stays intact as a historical record, per Knowledge Architecture.

docs.text:

docs.title: Knowledge Architecture
docs.text:
Version: 1.1.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document defines how knowledge is organized, where it lives, and how it is kept from decaying. W7 is, structurally, a knowledge organization before it is anything else — this is the architecture of that knowledge.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Documentation systems fail in predictable ways: the same fact is written in three places and only one gets updated; nobody knows which document is authoritative; old drafts are indistinguishable from current guidance; and eventually people stop trusting the documentation and start asking each other directly, which does not scale and does not survive anyone leaving.

This document exists to prevent that outcome, deliberately, before the repository grows large enough for it to happen by accident.

docs.title: One Fact, One Home
docs.text:
Every fact about W7 has exactly one canonical document. Every other document that needs that fact links to it instead of restating it.

Examples of canonical homes already established:

Fact Canonical home Why W7 exists, its mission and vision Constitution What "success" means Legacy How initiatives are created Initiative Framework How decisions get made Decision Framework Why a specific architectural choice was made The relevant ADR

When in doubt about whether to write something new or link to something existing, the answer is: search first, link if it exists, write only if it truly does not.

docs.title: Two Repositories, One Boundary
docs.text:
Knowledge about W7 lives in exactly two places, and they have different jobs.

GitHub (this repository and each initiative's repository) is the official, versioned, reviewable source of truth. If it isn't in GitHub, it isn't official — no exceptions, regardless of how complete or correct a note elsewhere might be.

Obsidian (Rafael OS) is personal knowledge management: drafts, half-formed ideas, private reflections, working notes that are not yet ready to be claims anyone else can rely on.

Obsidian never replaces GitHub. The moment a note in Obsidian is stable enough that someone else could reasonably act on it, it graduates into a Markdown document in the appropriate GitHub repository. Details on this boundary are in Information Boundaries.

docs.title: Status, Not Silence
docs.text:
Every document in this repository declares a Status in its header (Draft, Active, Deprecated, Superseded). A document with no status is a defect, not a stylistic omission — see the Documentation Standard.

Deprecated and Superseded documents are not deleted. History is kept and linked forward to whatever replaced them, the same way an ADR is never rewritten, only superseded by a new one. Deleting a document deletes the reasoning behind past decisions, which is exactly the knowledge a 10-year-old organization needs most.

docs.title: Discoverability Over Cleverness
docs.text:
Documents are organized by the layer they belong to (see Architecture Overview), not by team, date, or author. A new reader should be able to find any document by asking "which layer does this belong to?" rather than by remembering who wrote it or when.

Cross-references exist at the bottom of every document under a Related Documents heading, so that no document is an island reachable only from the README.

docs.text:

  • Documentation Standard — the concrete rules every document must follow
  • Information Boundaries — the GitHub / Obsidian boundary in detail
  • ADR Template — how a decision becomes permanent knowledge

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
Version: 1.1.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document explains how W7 is structured as a system, independent of any single initiative or product. It is the map that everything else in docs/architecture/, docs/framework/ and docs/initiatives/ fits into.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
W7 is not a single codebase, so its "architecture" is not a diagram of servers and databases. It is the structure of decisions, ownership and inheritance that lets many unrelated initiatives (WarTips today, others tomorrow) share one foundation without becoming tangled together or drifting apart.

An architecture document for an ecosystem like this has to answer one question well: when something changes, what else is forced to change with it, and what is protected from that change?

docs.title: The Layer Model
docs.text:
W7 is organized as ordered layers. Each layer may depend on the layers above it. No layer may depend on a layer below it.

Foundation
   ↓
Identity
   ↓
Governance
   ↓
Framework
   ↓
Initiatives
   ↓
Products
   ↓
Experiences
   ↓
Continuous Learning
Layer Answers Lives in Changes Foundation Why does W7 exist? docs/foundations/ Rarely, deliberately Identity How does W7 present itself? docs/identity/ Occasionally Governance Who decides, and how? docs/framework/governance.md Occasionally Framework How are initiatives and products created? docs/framework/ As patterns mature Initiatives What is currently being built? docs/initiatives/ Frequently Products What ships to users? Initiative-owned repositories Frequently Experiences What do people actually feel and use? Initiative-owned surfaces Continuously Continuous Learning What did we learn, and where does it feed back in? ADRs, retrospectives, this repository Continuously

A change at the bottom of the stack (an experience, a product feature) should never require a change at the top (the Constitution). A change at the top should be rare, and when it happens, it is expected to ripple downward.

docs.title: Inheritance, Not Duplication
docs.text:
Every initiative inherits from the Foundation and Identity layers by reference, not by copy.

WarTips does not restate the W7 philosophy in its own repository. It links to it. If the philosophy changes, every initiative's understanding of it changes at the same time, because there is exactly one copy.

Initiatives are free to extend what they inherit — a distinct voice, a distinct visual treatment, a distinct product decision — as long as the extension does not contradict the Foundation. Extension is welcome. Contradiction is not, and is resolved through the Decision Framework.

docs.title: This Repository's Job
docs.text:
project-w7 is the Foundation, Identity, Governance and Framework layers, plus a registry of Initiatives. It intentionally does not contain:

  • Product code (that lives in the owning initiative's repository or product surface)
  • Personal notes or drafts (that stays in Obsidian / Rafael OS, see Information Boundaries)
  • Anything that only makes sense to one initiative and no other

If a document only matters to WarTips, it belongs in WarTips' own repository, not here. If a document matters to every initiative that will ever exist under W7, it belongs here.

docs.title: Technology Stack
docs.text:
Version: 1.1.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document lists the tools W7 is built on at the foundation layer, and the reasoning behind each choice. It does not list technology choices made inside individual initiatives — those belong to the initiative's own repository and inherit only the principles below, not the specific tools.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The stack favors open formats, established tools and replaceable hosted services likely to remain recoverable in ten years. This is a deliberate bias. Trend-driven tooling and proprietary storage formats are liabilities in a repository meant to outlast whatever is popular the year it was written.

docs.title: Principles Behind the Choices
docs.text:
Open formats over proprietary ones. Anything that stores W7's knowledge must be readable with a text editor and a Git client alone, with no vendor account required to recover it.

Plain text over binary. Markdown, YAML and plain text diff cleanly, merge predictably, and survive tool migrations. Binary formats (proprietary word processors, design tool project files) are avoided for anything canonical.

Git as the mechanism, GitHub as the venue. The mechanism (Git) is portable and vendor-independent. The venue (GitHub) is replaceable if it ever needs to be, because the mechanism underneath it is not locked in.

Static over dynamic. Nothing in this repository requires a running server, a database, or an account to read. A clone of this repository, opened with any text editor, is fully self-contained.

docs.title: The Stack
docs.text: Layer Choice Why Source control Git Distributed, open, the de facto standard; not tied to any single host Hosting GitHub Where the team already collaborates; not treated as irreplaceable — see below Documentation format Markdown (CommonMark) Readable as plain text, renders everywhere, no proprietary lock-in Documentation site MkDocs (Material theme) Static site generator with no server dependency; builds directly from the Markdown already in this repository, nothing is duplicated to produce it Decision records ADRs (Markdown, template) Lightweight, versioned alongside the decisions they document Commit convention Conventional Commits Machine-parseable history; enables changelogs and makes intent explicit at a glance Continuous integration GitHub Actions Validates and deploys the documentation build on changes to main; public availability still depends on repository and Pages settings Personal knowledge management Obsidian ("Rafael OS") Explicitly not part of the stack that produces official documentation — see Information Boundaries

docs.title: What Is Deliberately Not Here
docs.text: There is no database, no backend service, and no build step that isn't a static site generator. If a future initiative needs any of those, it is that initiative's decision to make in its own repository, following the Product Framework — it does not become part of this repository's stack.

docs.title: Reversibility
docs.text: GitHub was chosen for convenience and reach, not because W7 depends on it existing forever. Everything in this repository is plain Markdown under Git; migrating hosts is a git remote set-url away, not a rewrite. This is intentional: the tool should always be easier to replace than the knowledge it holds.

docs.title: Ecosystem Topology
docs.text:
Version: 1.2.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document is a visual complement to Architecture Overview: the same layer model, repository structure and initiative inheritance rules, expressed as diagrams instead of tables and prose.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Architecture Overview explains the layer model in words. Some relationships — especially inheritance and the feedback loop back into the Foundation — are easier to verify correct as a diagram than as a table. This document exists so that "does this change respect the topology?" can be checked visually, not just argued in text.

docs.title: Layer Model
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    F["Foundation<br/>Why W7 exists"]
    I["Identity<br/>How W7 is expressed"]
    G["Governance<br/>Who decides"]
    FR["Framework<br/>How work is created"]
    IN["Initiatives<br/>Enduring areas of work"]
    P["Products<br/>Maintained outputs"]
    E["Experiences<br/>What people encounter"]
    L["Learning<br/>Evidence and ADRs"]

    F --> I --> G --> FR --> IN --> P --> E --> L
    L -.->|feeds back as an ADR or amendment| F

    classDef stable fill:#111111,stroke:#c8a45d,color:#ffffff,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef volatile fill:#f7f7f5,stroke:#666666,color:#111111;
    class F,I,G stable
    class FR,IN,P,E,L volatile

Dependencies only ever point downward (solid arrows). The only upward path is the dotted feedback loop — a lesson learned at any layer becomes an ADR, and only a deliberate, reviewed ADR is allowed to change the Foundation. See Decision Framework.

docs.title: Repository Structure
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    ROOT["project-w7<br/>Canonical ecosystem repository"]
    ROOT --> GOV["Governing layers"]
    ROOT --> WORK["Operating layers"]
    ROOT --> SUPPORT["Repository support"]

    GOV --> FOUND["foundations/"]
    GOV --> IDENT["identity/"]
    GOV --> FRAME["framework/"]

    WORK --> INIT["initiatives/"]
    WORK --> ARCH["architecture/"]
    WORK --> STD["standards/"]
    WORK --> ADR["adr/"]
    WORK --> ROAD["roadmap/"]
    WORK --> FOUNDER["founder/"]

    SUPPORT --> TEMPLATES["templates/"]
    SUPPORT --> SCRIPTS["scripts/"]
    SUPPORT --> GITHUB[".github/"]

    FOUND --> IDENT --> FRAME --> INIT
    STD -.-> GOV
    ADR -.-> GOV

Folder placement is not cosmetic — it is the mechanism that enforces the layer model in the previous diagram. A document in the wrong folder implies the wrong dependency direction. See ADR-0002.

docs.title: Initiative Inheritance
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    W7["W7<br/><small>Foundation + Identity + Governance + Framework</small>"]
    WT["WarTips<br/><small>Active initiative</small>"]
    F1["Future initiative<br/><small>e.g. Home Lab</small>"]
    F2["Future initiative<br/><small>e.g. Academy</small>"]

    W7 -->|inherits by reference, not copy| WT
    W7 -->|inherits by reference, not copy| F1
    W7 -->|inherits by reference, not copy| F2

    WT --> WTP1["Product<br/><small>none registered yet</small>"]
    F1 --> F1P["Products<br/><small>defined when created</small>"]
    F2 --> F2P["Products<br/><small>defined when created</small>"]

Every initiative points back to exactly one W7. No initiative points to another initiative — cross-initiative dependencies are deliberately not part of this topology. If one is ever needed, it is a Type 2/3 decision under the Decision Framework, not an informal link between two docs/initiatives/ folders.

docs.title: Knowledge Boundary
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Obsidian["Obsidian — Rafael OS"]
        drafts["Drafts, private reflections,<br/>working notes"]
    end
    subgraph GitHub["GitHub — official record"]
        official["Reviewed Markdown,<br/>versioned, linkable"]
    end

    drafts -->|graduates once stable enough<br/>for someone else to rely on| official
    official -.->|never flows back as private notes| drafts

This is a one-way graduation, never a sync. See Information Boundaries.

docs.title: W7 Constitution
docs.text:
Version: 1.1.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This Constitution defines the enduring principles every W7 initiative inherits and the questions that govern significant decisions across the ecosystem.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Products, technologies and organizational forms change more quickly than the principles behind them. W7 needs one stable foundation so its initiatives can evolve independently without losing the purpose that makes them part of the same ecosystem.

docs.title: Preamble
docs.text:
W7 exists to create meaningful initiatives that help people learn, build and evolve.

Knowledge becomes more valuable when it is organized.

Technology becomes more valuable when it empowers people.

Ideas become more valuable when they are shared.

This Constitution defines the enduring principles that guide every initiative created within W7.

Products may evolve.

Technologies may change.

The philosophy remains.

docs.title: Article I — Purpose
docs.text: The purpose of W7 is to transform complexity into clarity through systems, technology, education and thoughtful design.

docs.title: Article II — Mission
docs.text: Design initiatives that empower people through knowledge, engineering and continuous learning.

docs.title: Article III — Vision
docs.text: To become a long-term ecosystem recognized for building meaningful initiatives that improve the way people learn, collaborate and create.

docs.title: Article IV — Philosophy
docs.text:
Learning never ends.

Teaching accelerates learning.

Curiosity creates opportunity.

Humility enables growth.

Structure creates freedom.

People come before technology.

Progress is achieved through continuous improvement.

docs.title: Article V — Identity
docs.text:
W7 is the origin.

Every initiative inherits its philosophy, governance and identity.

Each initiative may develop its own products, audience, visual language and communication style while remaining aligned with the W7 principles.

docs.title: Article VI — Decision Framework
docs.text:
Every important decision must answer four questions.

Why should this exist?

Who benefits?

Will it remain valuable over time?

Does it strengthen the W7 ecosystem?

If any answer is no, the decision should be reconsidered.

docs.title: Article VII — Evolution
docs.text:
W7 is designed to evolve.

Its legal structure may change.

Its initiatives may grow.

Its products may come and go.

Its principles remain constant.

docs.title: Closing Statement
docs.text:
Build intentionally.

Share generously.

Lead with humility.

Enjoy the Journey.

docs.title: W7 Legacy
docs.text:
Version: 1.1.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document defines what W7 intends to leave behind after individual products, technologies and initiatives have ended or changed.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: W7 is designed for continuous evolution, so permanence cannot depend on any particular output. Legacy provides the long-term measure that remains useful when shorter-term measures such as adoption, visibility or product growth no longer apply.

docs.title: Legacy
docs.text:
Every initiative eventually ends.

Products evolve.

Technologies become obsolete.

Companies change.

People move on.

The only thing that truly remains is the impact we leave on others.

For W7, success is not measured solely by what we build.

It is measured by the lives we influence, the knowledge we share, the opportunities we create and the memories we build together.

Our work exists to make someone's journey a little shorter, a little clearer and a little more meaningful.

Because, in the end...

No achievement is greater than the people with whom we share the journey.

docs.title: Our Promise
docs.text:
We will build with excellence.

We will teach with humility.

We will learn continuously.

We will leave every place better than we found it.

And we will never forget why we started.

docs.title: Closing Statement
docs.text:
Enjoy the Journey.

With those you love.

docs.title: W7 Manifesto
docs.text:
Version: 1.1.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This Manifesto expresses the beliefs that shape how W7 learns, builds, teaches and measures impact.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Constitution defines W7's governing principles. This document gives those principles a human voice so contributors and initiatives can understand the intent behind the rules, not only the rules themselves.

docs.title: We believe...
docs.text:
Technology is one of humanity's greatest tools.

Not because of machines.

Not because of software.

Not because of artificial intelligence.

But because of what it enables people to become.

Knowledge changes lives.

Not when it is accumulated.

When it is shared.

Every lesson explained.

Every mistake documented.

Every discovery passed forward.

Makes someone else's journey shorter.

We believe complexity is inevitable.

Clarity is intentional.

The role of an engineer is not to make things look difficult.

It is to make difficult things understandable.

We reject knowledge as status.

We reject ego disguised as expertise.

We reject the idea that teaching diminishes mastery.

Teaching is mastery.

The best way to learn is to build.

The best way to understand is to explain.

The best way to grow is to help others grow.

Every initiative created under W7 exists for a single reason:

To leave the path a little shorter than we found it.

Whether through software.

Infrastructure.

Documentation.

Design.

Education.

Or simply one conversation.

We measure success differently.

Not by followers.

Not by titles.

Not by certifications.

Not by recognition.

But by impact.

How many people became more confident because something we built made their work easier?

How many people dared to try because someone explained without judgment?

How many people continued their journey because they realized they were capable?

Those are the metrics that matter.

We believe learning never ends.

Every answer creates a new question.

Every project reveals another opportunity.

Every achievement becomes the foundation for something greater.

Curiosity is not a phase.

It is a way of life.

W7 is not defined by a company.

It is not a single product.

It is more than a brand.

W7 is a commitment.

A commitment to learn continuously.

To build intentionally.

To teach generously.

To lead with humility.

And to create systems that empower people.

The destination will always change.

The journey never ends.

Enjoy the Journey.

docs.title: W7 Mission
docs.text:
Version: 1.0.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document states what W7 does now to move toward its long-term vision.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Constitution defines W7's authority and the Vision defines its destination. The Mission connects both to present action without prescribing a particular company form, product, or technology.

docs.title: Mission
docs.text:
W7 builds meaningful initiatives through engineering, technology, design, and education.

It turns knowledge into durable systems, useful products, and clear learning experiences. It does so with intention, shares what can help others, and keeps technology accountable to the people it serves.

docs.title: Mission in Practice
docs.text:
W7 fulfills this mission by:

  • capturing and refining knowledge before it is lost;
  • creating initiatives around a clear, lasting purpose;
  • applying engineering discipline to both technical and non-technical work;
  • teaching from real experience rather than manufactured authority;
  • designing systems that can evolve without abandoning their principles; and
  • measuring progress by usefulness, learning, and positive impact rather than activity alone.

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text: The mission does not require W7 to become a particular kind of organization. It may support open-source work, education, consulting, products, research, or other forms when they satisfy the Constitution and the Initiative Framework.

docs.title: W7 Operating Model
docs.text:
Version: 1.0.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document explains how W7 converts its Foundation into governed initiatives and useful outcomes.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: W7 is an ecosystem and operating model, not a promise to adopt one legal form or business model. A shared sequence keeps new work coherent without centralizing every initiative-level decision.

docs.title: The Model
docs.text:
Foundation → Identity → Governance → Framework → Initiatives → Products → Experiences

Each layer inherits constraints from the layers to its left. A downstream layer may specialize them but may not contradict them.

Layer Question Canonical home Foundation Why do we exist and how do we behave? docs/foundations/ Identity How is belonging to W7 expressed? docs/identity/ Governance Who decides and how is change approved? docs/framework/governance.md Framework How are decisions, initiatives, and products created? docs/framework/ Initiatives What enduring areas of work exist? docs/initiatives/ Products What maintained outputs does an initiative own? Initiative repository Experiences How do people encounter the output? Product or initiative repository

docs.title: Operating Cycle
docs.text:
1. Capture: collect observations and ideas; personal notes may begin in Rafael OS, but have no official authority.
  2. Clarify: define purpose, beneficiary, boundaries, evidence, and expected value.
  3. Decide: classify the decision and record an ADR when required.
  4. Build: create the smallest useful outcome under the relevant standards.
  5. Validate: review correctness, consistency, security, usability, and documentation.
  6. Publish: commit the canonical result to the owning GitHub repository.
  7. Learn: observe outcomes and feed evidence into the next cycle.

docs.title: Source of Truth
docs.text: GitHub repositories hold W7's official record. Rafael OS is limited to personal knowledge management and early capture, as defined by Information Boundaries; content becomes official only after review and commit.

docs.title: Measures of Health
docs.text: W7 evaluates the model through purpose alignment, maintained knowledge, decision traceability, initiative autonomy, useful outcomes, and the absence of avoidable dependency or information risk.

docs.title: Principles of Building
docs.text:
Version: 1.0.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document defines the principles W7 applies when turning an idea into an initiative, product, document, or experience.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Values describe how W7 behaves. These principles translate those values into practical choices during creation.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. Begin with purpose. State who benefits, what changes for them, and why the work should exist before selecting tools or formats.
  2. Understand before automating. Automation should encode a process that is already understood; it must not conceal uncertainty.
  3. Make the smallest useful thing. Reduce scope until real value can be tested without building disposable complexity.
  4. Prefer evidence to assumption. Inspect the current state, test the riskiest claim, and record what was learned.
  5. Design for change. Keep boundaries clear, decisions reversible where possible, and durable decisions documented.
  6. Keep people accountable. Tools may accelerate work, but a named human owns every published decision and outcome.
  7. Make knowledge transferable. Document context and reasoning so the work can outlive the person or tool that created it.
  8. Protect trust. Privacy, security, consent, accessibility, and honest communication are requirements, not later refinements.
  9. Finish deliberately. Validate against the stated purpose, remove placeholders, and make the resulting state explicit.
  10. Enjoy the journey. Build at a sustainable pace and preserve room for curiosity, relationships, and learning.

docs.title: Definition of Meaningful
docs.text: Work is meaningful when it serves a real person or community, has a defensible reason to exist, can remain useful beyond its launch, and strengthens rather than fragments the W7 ecosystem.

docs.title: W7 Values
docs.text:
Version: 1.0.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document defines the values used to judge how W7 works, especially when several valid paths are available.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Values are behavioral commitments, not promotional words. Each value below includes the observable behavior expected from W7 and its initiatives.

docs.title: Curiosity
docs.text: We ask before assuming, test before declaring, and remain willing to revise a belief when evidence changes.

docs.title: Clarity
docs.text: We turn complexity into explanations, decisions, and systems that others can understand and maintain.

docs.title: Craft
docs.text: We care about correctness, usability, and the details that make work durable. We improve through deliberate iteration rather than chasing perfection before learning.

docs.title: Generosity
docs.text: We share knowledge that can help others, credit the work we build upon, and create conditions in which people can grow.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text: We accept ownership for decisions and outcomes. Human judgment remains accountable even when tools, automation, or AI contribute.

docs.title: Continuity
docs.text: We build for a future reader and maintainer. Open formats, documented reasoning, and transferable knowledge matter more than short-lived convenience.

docs.title: Joy in the Journey
docs.text: We value the process and the people who share it, not only the destination. Sustainable pace, relationships, and learning are part of success.

docs.title: Using the Values
docs.text: When values appear to conflict, the Constitution and Information Boundaries take precedence. The Decision Framework records the trade-off instead of pretending it did not exist.

docs.title: W7 Vision
docs.text:
Version: 1.1.0

Status: Active

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document defines the long-term direction W7 uses to evaluate whether its initiatives are creating the kind of impact the ecosystem exists to pursue.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Constitution states the destination at a governing level. This document expands that direction into a durable picture of success without turning it into a fixed roadmap or tying it to a particular product, technology or organizational form.

docs.title: Vision
docs.text:
To become a timeless ecosystem where meaningful initiatives are created, nurtured and shared to help people grow.

We envision a future where W7 is recognized not by the number of products it creates, but by the positive impact those initiatives have on people, communities and organizations.

Every initiative within W7 should make knowledge more accessible, technology more understandable and growth more achievable.

Our ambition is not to build everything.

Our ambition is to build the right things, in the right way, for the right reasons.

We believe that long-term value is created through consistency, curiosity and generosity.

If, decades from now, people remember W7 as a place that empowered others to learn, build and share, then we will have fulfilled our vision.

docs.title: Success
docs.text:
Success is measured by impact, not scale.

By trust, not attention.

By legacy, not popularity.

docs.title: Closing Statement
docs.text:
Create initiatives that outlive trends.

Build systems that outlive products.

Inspire people who will build what comes next.

Enjoy the Journey.

docs.title: Founder's Letter
docs.text:
Version: 1.1.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This is a personal letter, not an operational document. It exists to say, in my own words, why I built W7 and what I want it to mean to whoever reads it — today, or long after I've handed it to someone else, or stepped back from it entirely.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The Foundation documents state W7's principles in a form others can apply. This letter preserves the founder's personal intent behind those principles without replacing or extending their operational meaning.

To whoever is reading this,

If you're reading this as a collaborator, a future version of myself, or simply someone curious about what W7 actually is underneath the folders and the framework documents — this letter is for you.

I didn't start W7 because I had a business plan. I started it because I noticed a pattern in my own life: the moments I valued most were never the moments I solved something alone. They were the moments I explained something to someone else and watched it make sense to them. A fix that took me an entire night of frustration, turned into a five-minute explanation that saved someone else that same night. That trade always felt like the better deal.

I also noticed the opposite pattern, in myself and in people I respect: knowledge hoarded quietly, out of habit more than intention, because writing it down properly always seemed like something to do later. Later rarely comes on its own. W7 is my attempt to make "later" the default instead of the exception.

I called it W7 instead of naming it after a single product because I didn't want to build one thing. I wanted to build the conditions under which many meaningful things could exist — some I can picture today, most I can't yet. That's why this repository is full of structure before it's full of products: WarTips is real and active, but the framework around it was written so that whatever comes after WarTips doesn't have to start from zero, and doesn't have to inherit my mistakes by copying them instead of by choice.

I want to be honest about something else: I don't know exactly what W7 will become. It might stay something I build alongside a career. It might grow into something bigger. The Constitution is written so that either outcome — and everything in between — is fine, because what actually matters isn't the shape it takes. It's whether the people who encounter it walk away having learned something, taught something, or trusted something a little more than before.

If you take one thing from this letter, let it be this: build the thing that makes someone else's path a little easier, document it honestly, and don't wait for permission to start. I didn't.

Enjoy the Journey. With those you love.

— Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Origin Story
docs.text:
Version: 1.1.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document tells the story of how W7 started — not as marketing, but as an honest account for anyone who wants to understand where the philosophy in the Constitution and Manifesto actually came from.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: W7's operational documents explain what the ecosystem is and how it works. This account preserves the sequence of habits and decisions that led to those documents, without giving the story authority over the active Foundation.

docs.title: Before W7 Had a Name
docs.text:
Long before there was a repository, a Constitution, or a name, there was a habit: writing things down after solving them. Not for anyone else at first — just so the next time the same problem showed up, the answer wouldn't have to be rebuilt from memory. Some of those notes turned into conversations. Some of those conversations turned into someone else solving their own version of the same problem faster than they would have otherwise.

That habit is the actual origin of W7. Everything else — the name, the structure, this repository — came later, as a way of taking that habit seriously enough to make it repeatable and shareable, instead of something that only existed in one person's private notes.

docs.title: Why WarTips First
docs.text: WarTips came before W7 had a formal structure, because it was the most direct expression of that habit: practical knowledge, earned the hard way, written down so someone else doesn't have to earn it the same way twice. It stayed the first initiative deliberately, even after the rest of the framework was written, because it's proof that the philosophy produces something real — not just documentation about documentation.

docs.title: Why a Constitution Before a Product
docs.text: It would have been faster to skip straight to building more products under the WarTips name and let a philosophy emerge from whatever got built. That path was considered and rejected. Products built without a clear "why" tend to drift toward whatever is easiest to build next, not toward what was actually meant to matter. Writing the Constitution, the Manifesto and the Legacy first was slower, and deliberately so — it meant that whatever got built next would have to justify itself against something that already existed, rather than the other way around.

docs.title: Why the Name W7
docs.text: W7 was chosen to mean something broader than any single product or even any single person's career — an ecosystem, not a brand tied to one offering. The name is deliberately abstract enough to hold a personal project, a consulting practice, or something larger, without needing to be renamed when the shape of it changes. See Constitution, Article VII, for why that flexibility was written in as a principle rather than left implicit.

docs.title: Where This Leaves Us
docs.text: This repository is the direct continuation of that original habit: solve something, understand it well enough to explain it, write it down properly, and make sure the next person — including a future version of the person who wrote it — doesn't have to start over. Everything else documented here exists to make that easier to do consistently, at whatever scale W7 eventually reaches.

docs.title: Decision Framework
docs.text:
Version: 1.1.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document defines how decisions are made within W7, so that judgment calls are consistent even as the people making them, or the number of people involved, changes over time.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A single founder can hold an entire decision-making process in their head and never notice it is a process. That stops being true the moment a second person, a collaborator, or a future team needs to make a decision the same way Rafael would have. Writing the process down now, while it is still simple, is cheaper than reconstructing it later under pressure.

docs.title: The Four Questions
docs.text:
The Constitution, Article VI, establishes four questions that any significant decision must answer:

  1. Why should this exist?
  2. Who benefits?
  3. Will it remain valuable over time?
  4. Does it strengthen the W7 ecosystem?

If any answer is genuinely no, the decision should be reconsidered before it is made, not after it ships.

This document operationalizes those four questions into something usable in practice.

docs.title: What Counts as "Significant"
docs.text:
Not every decision needs this framework. Day-to-day implementation choices inside an initiative do not. A decision goes through this framework when it does at least one of the following:

  • Changes the Foundation, Identity, Governance or Framework layers
  • Creates a new initiative or discontinues an existing one
  • Introduces a dependency, tool, or convention that other initiatives will be expected to inherit
  • Cannot be easily reversed within a normal iteration cycle

When in doubt, write an ADR. Writing it down is the cheapest way to find out whether a decision was actually significant.

docs.title: The Process
docs.text:
1. State the decision as a question, not as a conclusion already reached. "Should WarTips adopt a paid tier?" not "WarTips will have a paid tier."
  2. Answer the four Constitutional questions explicitly, in writing.
  3. List the alternatives considered, including "do nothing." A decision with no alternatives listed has usually not been examined closely enough.
  4. Record the decision as an ADR if it meets the significance criteria above, using the ADR Template.
  5. Let the decision breathe. Significant, hard-to-reverse decisions are not made in the same sitting they are proposed in, when that is practical.

docs.title: Reversibility as a First-Class Property
docs.text:
Every decision is classified by how expensive it is to reverse:

Class Meaning Example Type 1 Easily reversible Choice of a linter, a document's structure Type 2 Reversible with real cost A framework convention adopted by multiple initiatives Type 3 Effectively irreversible A change to the Constitution, discontinuing an initiative's identity

Type 1 decisions should be made quickly and without ceremony. Type 3 decisions deserve the full process above, deliberately slowed down. Treating a Type 1 decision like a Type 3 one is as much a failure of judgment as the reverse.

docs.title: Disagreement
docs.text: W7 is designed to scale from one person to many. When more than one person is involved in a decision and they disagree, the tie-breaker is whichever answer better satisfies the four Constitutional questions — not seniority, not who spoke first. If the disagreement is about the Constitution itself, it is resolved through Governance, not through this framework.

docs.text:

  • Governance — who holds decision-making authority at each layer
  • ADR Template — how a significant decision is recorded permanently
  • Initiative Framework and Product Framework — the two most common places this framework is applied

docs.title: Governance
docs.text:
Version: 1.1.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document defines who has authority over each layer of W7, and how that authority is expected to change as the ecosystem grows from one person to a team, a company, or an open-source community.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Governance written for a single founder is easy to get wrong in two opposite directions: over-formalizing a process that today is just one person's judgment, or under-specifying it so badly that it cannot survive that person stepping back, delegating, or bringing in collaborators. This document aims for the minimum structure that is still true today and still correct if W7 grows.

docs.title: Authority by Layer
docs.text:
Authority follows the layer model in Architecture Overview: the higher the layer, the narrower and more deliberate the authority to change it.

Layer Who can propose changes Who approves Foundation Anyone contributing to W7 Founder (today); a designated Foundation steward in the future Identity Anyone contributing to W7 Founder or whoever holds brand ownership Governance Anyone contributing to W7 Founder; requires an ADR Framework Anyone contributing to W7 Founder or framework maintainers Initiatives Initiative maintainers Initiative lead, within the bounds of the Framework Products Product maintainers Product/initiative lead

An initiative lead has full authority over their own initiative's products and experiences. They do not have authority to change the Foundation, Identity or Framework layers unilaterally — those changes go through the Decision Framework because they affect every other initiative too.

docs.title: Today's Model
docs.text:
As of this writing, W7 has a single founder who holds authority at every layer. This is stated explicitly rather than left implicit, because an unstated single point of authority is indistinguishable from a system with no governance at all — and both fail the same way if that person is unavailable.

The table above is written for the organization W7 is designed to become, not only the one it is today, so that adding a second contributor or an initiative lead is a matter of assigning a role that already exists in this document, not inventing one under pressure.

docs.title: Amending the Constitution
docs.text:
The Constitution is the one document with a higher bar than the table above implies. A Constitutional amendment:

  1. Must be proposed in writing, stating which Article changes and why.
  2. Must be recorded as an ADR, regardless of how small it seems.
  3. Takes effect only after the founder (or, in the future, whichever governance body holds Foundation authority) explicitly approves it.
  4. Never happens silently as a side effect of another change.

docs.title: New Initiatives and New Contributors
docs.text: Bringing in a new initiative or a new contributor with governance authority is itself a Type 2 or Type 3 decision under the Decision Framework, and is expected to update this document's tables when it happens — this document is written to be edited, not treated as immutable the way the Constitution is.

docs.text:

  • Decision Framework — the process this document assigns authority over
  • Initiative Framework — how initiative leads acquire their authority in the first place
  • Architecture Overview — the layer model authority is organized around

docs.title: Initiative Framework
docs.text:
Version: 1.1.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document defines what an initiative is, how a new one is created under W7, and what it inherits versus what it is free to define for itself.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: WarTips is the first initiative. It will not be the last. Without a written framework, each new initiative would be created by copying whatever WarTips happened to do, mistakes included, and the reasoning behind W7's structure would have to be reverse-engineered every time. This document is written so that the second, fifth and twentieth initiative can be started with the same clarity as the first.

docs.title: What an Initiative Is
docs.text:
An initiative is a distinct effort — technical, educational, creative or otherwise — created under the W7 ecosystem to pursue a specific purpose, with its own audience, its own cadence, and typically its own repository.

An initiative is not a legal entity, a product, or a team. It may eventually contain several products (see Product Framework), or none yet. WarTips today is a single initiative expressed through documentation and content; it may grow into several products later without becoming a different initiative.

docs.title: What Every Initiative Inherits
docs.text:
Every initiative, without exception, inherits from the layers above it in Architecture Overview:

  • The Constitution, Manifesto, Vision and Legacy — by reference, never by copy.
  • The W7 Identity rules for how it relates to the master brand.
  • The Governance model, at least until it earns enough scale to warrant its own initiative-specific governance layer.
  • The Documentation, Engineering and GitHub standards.

docs.title: What Every Initiative Defines for Itself
docs.text:
• Its own name, voice and visual expression, within the bounds of the Identity layer.
  • Its own audience, cadence, and choice of products.
  • Its own technology choices, following the principles (not the specific tools) in Technology Stack.
  • Its own repository, issue tracker and release process when its work requires them.

An initiative that finds itself needing to contradict a Foundation-layer principle to succeed is a signal to raise that contradiction through the Decision Framework — not to quietly diverge.

docs.title: Creating a New Initiative
docs.text:
1. State the purpose. One paragraph: what this initiative exists to do that no existing initiative already covers.
  2. Answer the Constitution's four questions (Article VI) for the initiative as a whole, not just for a single product inside it.
  3. Register it in docs/initiatives/<initiative-name>/README.md in this repository, using templates/initiative-template.md. WarTips is the first completed example, not the template itself.
  4. Add it to the ecosystem table in the root README.md and to the Roadmap if it is not yet active.
  5. Create the initiative's own repository, if it needs one, following the GitHub Standard.

A new initiative does not need permission to exist experimentally — it needs this process before it is presented as an official, active part of the W7 ecosystem.

docs.title: Retiring an Initiative
docs.text: Initiatives end. That is expected, not a failure (see Legacy). Retiring one means: marking its entry Status: Retired in docs/initiatives/, keeping its documentation rather than deleting it, and recording the decision as an ADR if the initiative had any dependents relying on it.

docs.title: Product Framework
docs.text:
Version: 1.1.0

Status: Active

Owner: Rafael da Silva Guerra

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document defines what a product is within W7, how it differs from an initiative, and how a new product is created inside an existing initiative.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: An initiative is a purpose. A product is a concrete thing built to serve that purpose — a course, a tool, a piece of software, a written guide, a service. One initiative may have several products, or none yet, or products that come and go while the initiative itself continues. Without this distinction, "should this be its own initiative or just something WarTips ships" becomes a recurring, unresolved argument.

docs.title: Product vs. Initiative
docs.text:
Initiative Product Answers What is this effort for? What did we actually build? Lifespan Long-lived, may span years Often shorter; may be retired independently of the initiative Example WarTips A specific WarTips guide series, tool, or course Governed by Initiative Framework This document

A product always belongs to exactly one initiative. If something seems to belong to none of the existing initiatives, that is a signal to evaluate it as a new initiative, not an orphaned product.

docs.title: Creating a New Product
docs.text:
1. Identify the owning initiative. A product without an initiative is not created — either it fits one, or the Initiative Framework is used first.
  2. State the problem it solves for the initiative's audience, in concrete terms, not aspirational ones.
  3. Answer the Constitution's four questions (Article VI) at the product level: this is usually a lighter pass than the initiative-level version, but it is not skipped.
  4. Choose its technology deliberately, following the principles in Technology Stack rather than defaulting to whatever is trending.
  5. Register it in the owning initiative's entry in project-w7, then keep detailed product documentation in that initiative's own repository or documentation section. WarTips currently has no formally registered product.

docs.title: What a Product Inherits
docs.text: A product inherits everything its initiative inherits (see Initiative Framework), plus whatever conventions its initiative has additionally established. It does not get to skip the Engineering Standard or Documentation Standard because it is "just a small thing" — small things are exactly what accumulates into an unmaintainable ecosystem if left unstandardized.

docs.title: Product Lifecycle
docs.text:
Products move through four stages, and every product's documentation must state which stage it is in:

Stage Meaning Exploring Being validated; may be discarded without ceremony Active Built, maintained, and the initiative's current focus Maintained Stable, not actively developed further, but supported Retired No longer maintained; documentation kept for historical continuity

Retiring a product does not require retiring its initiative, and retiring an initiative does not erase the record of the products it shipped — see Legacy.

docs.text:
